\chapter{Numbers, and How Old You Are}
\label{ch:numbers-and-age}
\hlchaptermodality{47}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from one through ten and use singular forms of tener to ask and answer age with a number I know.}

Count from one through ten, move among tengo, tienes, and tiene, then ask and answer age with the number frame taught in the chapter.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco]{uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — counting to five}

\label{lesson:ES-C08-numeros-1-5}



\begin{quote}
Numbers are among the most reusable words in any language. Spanish keeps them close enough to Latin that English cousins can help you remember them. This lesson asks for only \textbf{five}: \textbf{uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ue} — \textbf{cuatro} begins \emph{KWA-}.
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — give \emph{tres} and \emph{cuatro} one light tap, not an English \emph{r}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{Latin source} & \textbf{English memory hook} \\
\midrule
\textbf{uno} (1) & \emph{ūnus} & \textbf{unit}, unique \\
\textbf{dos} (2) & \emph{duo} & \textbf{duo}, dual \\
\textbf{tres} (3) & \emph{trēs} & \textbf{trio}, triple \\
\textbf{cuatro} (4) & \emph{quattuor} & \textbf{quart}, quarter \\
\textbf{cinco} (5) & \emph{quīnque} & \textbf{quintet}, quintuplet \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The spellings changed, but the family resemblance remains. \emph{Cinco} and \emph{quintet} both descend from \emph{quīnque}; Spanish changed the opening sound while English borrowed a more visibly Latin form.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: uno becomes un or una}]
When \textbf{uno} stands alone, it means “one.” Before a noun it shortens:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{un} before a masculine noun: \textbf{un café} — one coffee / a coffee.
  \item \textbf{una} before a feminine noun: \textbf{una noche} — one night / a night.
\end{itemize}

This shortening is called \textbf{apocope}: the end drops away. Spanish uses the same forms for “one” and “a/an”; context supplies the difference.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco” — once up, once down
  \item “uno/unit, dos/duo, tres/trio, cuatro/quart, cinco/quintet”
  \item “un café, una noche” — hear \emph{uno} shorten
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give 1–5 in Spanish. (\emph{Uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco}.) Which English word helps you remember \emph{cinco}? (\emph{Quintet}, through Latin \emph{quīnque}.) What happens to \emph{uno} before a noun? (It becomes \textbf{un} or \textbf{una}.) Next: \textbf{six through ten}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez]{seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez — and the calendar's old count}

\label{lesson:ES-C08-numeros-6-10}



\begin{quote}
You can count to five. Add one small set and you reach ten: \textbf{seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez}. Four English month names will help hold the last four in memory.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ie} — \textbf{siete} begins \emph{SYE-}.
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ue} — \textbf{nueve} begins \emph{NWE-}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{Latin source} & \textbf{English memory hook} \\
\midrule
\textbf{seis} (6) & \emph{sex} & \textbf{sextet} \\
\textbf{siete} (7) & \emph{septem} & \textbf{September}, septet \\
\textbf{ocho} (8) & \emph{octō} & \textbf{October}, octave \\
\textbf{nueve} (9) & \emph{novem} & \textbf{November} \\
\textbf{diez} (10) & \emph{decem} & \textbf{December}, decimal \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say the chain aloud: \emph{siete–September, ocho–October, nueve–November, diez–December}. It is a memory path, not a second list to memorize.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The month names preserve an old Roman count in which \textbf{March was first}: September through December occupied positions seven through ten. When January and February stood before March, those names shifted to positions nine through twelve but kept their old numbers.

One tempting story is wrong: July and August were not new months inserted into the middle. The existing months \textbf{Quintilis} and \textbf{Sextilis} were later \textbf{renamed} for Julius Caesar and Augustus. The calendar moved; the numbered names stayed.

Numbers above ten belong to a later chapter. For now, stop cleanly at \textbf{diez}.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item count from \emph{uno} through \emph{diez}
  \item “siete/September, ocho/October, nueve/November, diez/December”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give 6–10. (\emph{Seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez}.) Why does \emph{December} carry the old word for ten? (The month names preserve a March-first count.) What happened to Quintilis and Sextilis? (They were renamed July and August.) Next: the verb \textbf{tener}, “to have.”
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tener]{tener — “to have,” with two visible changes}

\label{lesson:ES-C08-tener}



\begin{quote}
Regular \emph{comer} gave you \emph{como, comes, come}. The common verb \textbf{tener}, “to have,” belongs to the same \textbf{-er} family, but its three singular forms change in two places. Learn only those three today.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ie} — \textbf{tienes} begins \emph{TYE-}.
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — one light tap at the end of \textbf{tener}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{tener} descends from Latin \textbf{tenēre}, “to hold or keep.” Having is, at root, holding. English borrowed the same root many times:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{tenant}, \textbf{tenure}, \textbf{tenacious} — holding land, office, or position.
  \item \textbf{contain}, \textbf{retain}, \textbf{maintain}, \textbf{sustain} — holding together, back, in hand, or up.
\end{itemize}

When you see \emph{-tain} in English, think of Spanish \textbf{tener}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three singular forms}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{regular \emph{comer}} & \textbf{irregular \emph{tener}} \\
\midrule
yo & como & \textbf{tengo} \\
tú & comes & \textbf{tienes} \\
él / ella / usted & come & \textbf{tiene} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two small changes do all the work:

1. \textbf{yo} adds \textbf{g}: \emph{tengo}, not \emph{teno}. 2. The other two singular forms change \textbf{e $\to$ ie}: \emph{tienes, tiene}.

Later chapters will expand both patterns. For now, hold only \textbf{tengo, tienes, tiene} — the same three-person frame you already use for regular verbs.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “tener — tengo, tienes, tiene”
  \item “tener / tenant / retain” — the shared idea is \emph{hold}
  \item compare “como, comes, come” with “tengo, tienes, tiene”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{tenēre} mean? (“To hold.”) Give the three singular forms. (\emph{Tengo, tienes, tiene}.) What are the two changes? (\emph{g} appears in \emph{tengo}; \emph{e} becomes \emph{ie} in \emph{tienes/tiene}.) Next: use them to ask and answer about \textbf{age}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[¿Cuántos años tienes?]{¿Cuántos años tienes? — asking age}

\label{lesson:ES-C08-cuantos-anos}



\begin{quote}
You now have \emph{tengo, tienes, tiene} and the numbers one through ten. Put them together and you can ask or answer age. Spanish frames age as something you \textbf{have}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{¿Cuántos años tienes?} “How old are you?” — literally, “How many years do you have?”
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{cuántos} means “how many.” Latin \textbf{quantus}, “how much,” also gives English \textbf{quantity, quantum, quantify}.
  \item \textbf{años} means “years.” Latin \textbf{annus} also gives \textbf{annual} and \textbf{anniversary}. Its doubled \emph{nn} became Spanish \textbf{ñ}, exactly as your script lesson showed.
  \item \textbf{tienes} is the \emph{tú} form of \textbf{tener}.
\end{itemize}

Keep the marks visible: opening \textbf{¿}, the accent in \textbf{cuántos}, and the letter \textbf{ñ} in \textbf{años} each carries information.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Spanish “has” years}]
English says “I \textbf{am} ten years old.” Spanish says:

\begin{quote}
— ¿Cuántos años \textbf{tienes}? — \textbf{Tengo diez años.}
\end{quote}

The reusable frame is \textbf{Tengo + number + años}. Use a number you already know: \emph{Tengo ocho años}, \emph{Tengo nueve años}, \emph{Tengo diez años}. Larger numbers wait until their own lesson; the grammar does not change.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “¿Cuántos años tienes?”
  \item “Tengo ocho años. Tengo nueve años. Tengo diez años.”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the question literally ask? (“How many years do you have?”) Which verb carries age? (\emph{Tener}.) How do \emph{cuántos} and \emph{años} connect to English? (\emph{Quantus} $\to$ quantity; \emph{annus} $\to$ annual.) Next: combine counting, \emph{tener}, and age in one short exchange.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — counting, having, and age}

\label{lesson:ES-C08-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint asks for three small moves: count to ten, choose the right singular form of \emph{tener}, and use the age frame. Everything here has already appeared.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: count and conjugate}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Count: \textbf{uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez}.
  \item Change person: \textbf{tengo · tienes · tiene}.
  \item Remember the roots: \emph{quīnque} helps with \emph{cinco}; \emph{decem} helps with \emph{diez}; \emph{tenēre}, “hold,” helps with \emph{tener}.
  \item Keep the calendar correction: July and August were \textbf{renamed}, not inserted.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{The exchange — use only what you know}
\begin{quote}
— Hola. ¿Cómo te llamas? — Me llamo Ana. ¿Cuántos años tienes? — Tengo diez años. ¿Y tú? — Tengo nueve años.
\end{quote}

The exchange reuses the name question you already know, then adds exactly one new capability: age with \textbf{tener}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{uno through diez}, with Latin and English hooks instead of an isolated list.
  \item \textbf{un / una} before a noun, where standalone \emph{uno} shortens.
  \item \textbf{tengo, tienes, tiene}, the three singular forms of \textbf{tener}.
  \item \textbf{¿Cuántos años tienes? — Tengo … años}, with \emph{quantus/quantity} and \emph{annus/annual} showing where the words came from.
\end{itemize}

Numbers above ten and the plural forms of \emph{tener} remain deliberately deferred.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item count 1–10 up, then down
  \item “tengo, tienes, tiene”
  \item ask and answer age with a number from 1–10
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} “¿Cuántos años tienes? — Tengo nueve años.”

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to ten. Give the three singular forms of \emph{tener}. Ask “How old are you?” and answer with a number you learned. You can now move from a name exchange into one concrete personal detail. Next: the two Spanish ways to say “to be,” introduced one contrast at a time.
\end{tcolorbox}
